tells: 'remain an ongoing conversation among our ʿulamaʾ' — abstract, padded diction; Author A would write plainly, e.g. 'our ʿulamaʾ still differ on the finer questions'
'this book presents each view with neutrality' — nominalised, wordy construction; Author A would write 'this book gives each view'

'Three guiding principles frame the discussions in the chapters that follow' — academic register ('frame the discussions'); Author A says simply what follows, e.g. 'Three principles run through the chapters that follow'
'How this position differs from that of the Sufi orders is explored in Chapter Nine' — passive, report-style signposting; Author A uses active verbs ('Chapter Eight sets out', 'Chapter One reached')
Plain declaratives, Sheikh's line paraphrased then explained ('it is the law lived from the inside'), active chapter pointer ('Chapter Eight sets out their wider concerns') as in Author A

Picks up the previous verse, reports the Sheikh with 'he says', introduces and explains the Khomeini quotation, and links back ('Chapter One reached the same conclusion by another road') in Author A's manner
'asks why a believer should bother' — informal spoken phrasing; Author A would write 'asks why a believer should go beyond the obligations'
'with the goal of ʿirfan already on our lips in our duʿas' — decorative idiom; Author A states it flatly, e.g. 'with the goal of ʿirfan already named in our duʿas'
'the journey towards ʿirfan: the self' / 'keeps the traveller safe: the shariʿa' — colon held back for a reveal; Author A names the thing first and uses colons for lists
'with a compatible view of similarities to Sufism' — muddy abstract phrase; Author A would say plainly how Shia ʿirfan relates to Sufism
'as an endeavour for the ordinary believer' — stilted, abstract diction; Author A would write 'for ordinary believers to say'

'is often less practised' — vague hedged passive; Author A would say who neglects it and how
